newsitem.title: USA: Swiss official defends actions on Jewish funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss official defends actions on Jewish funds.

text.p: A Swiss government official on Wednesday defended his country's new effort to trace money in its banks claimed by families of Jewish Holocaust victims, declaring that "no penny should remain in Switzerland."

Thomas Borer, head of a Swiss task force coordinating an investigation into the funds, was testifying in an unusual appearance before a U.S. congressional committee amid considerable scepticism about the Swiss effort.
"We are fully aware that nothing less than our reputation as an honourable country ... is at stake," he said.
He said that in preparation for the hearing by the House of Representatives Banking Committee he had visited Washington's Holocaust Museum "to reflect on whether I am doing enough."

Switzerland has been subjected to months of negative publicity that has painted the neutral country as a willing partner of the Nazis in World War II. Critics have accused authorities of footdragging in seeking to track down funds and valuables of Jews and others left in dormant accounts.
Borer promised a swift investigation by an independent commission being set up by the Swiss parliament that would include a substantial number of non-Swiss and Jewish experts.

He said the Swiss government would make every effort to return wrongfully held assets to their rightful owners. If the owners could not be traced the money would be made available to "relevant charities," he said.
The official said banking secrecy laws were being waived for five years but it was intended to conclude the investigation in two to three years.

Senator Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican who has taken the lead in seeking to expose questionable activities by the Swiss in the past, made clear he felt this was too long, noting that many Holocaust survivors were in their eighties.
"What kind of confidence does that give us?" D'Amato asked the committee. "It suggests that the stonewalling continues."
Edgar Bronfman, president of the World Jewish Congress, questioned the role of the banks in the investigation, saying, "I am not convinced in my heart and soul that they are totally cooperating."

Bronfman also called for "a good faith financial gesture" by Switzerland that would not prejudice any final settlement but would ensure that ageing Holocaust survivors could get "some measure of justice" during their lifetimes.

While the commission of experts is seeking to trace funds in Swiss banks, a U.S. Government task force is conducting a historical examination of the issue of Nazi assets, including hoards of gold, that is expected to shed light on the role of the Swiss banks.
Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstadt, the investigation's coordinator, said a preliminary report was expected at the beginning of February.

A third investigation, focusing on dormant or heirless accounts in Swiss banks, is under way by a committee of "eminent persons" chaired by former U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Paul Volcker and including three Swiss Bankers Association members and three members chosen by the World Jewish Congress.

D'Amato and several Banking Committee members questioned past actions by Swiss governments, including agreements with communist ruled Poland and Hungary under which Holocaust victims' bank accounts were liquidated.
Borer said a final report on this issue was expected before the end of the month.

At the start of the hearing, Committee Chairman James Leach, an Iowa Republican, denied that it was driven by politics, noting that Swiss journalists' had asked about his motives. He described the aim as full disclosure and justice.
